29.title: Lost for three days (Luke 2:41–52)
29.hook: twelve-year-old Jesus stays in the Temple and asks why they didn't know he'd be in his Father's house
29.howItsDone: Catholics meditate on this story as the fifth joyful mystery of the rosary, the Finding in the Temple, and as one of the Seven Sorrows of Mary; it is read on the feast of the Holy Family.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Epiphany: strangers from the east, and a family running for Egypt. Your line was: the holy family were refugees. Week five starts now: the beginning. Day twenty-nine.
screen: `THE HOLY FAMILY WERE REFUGEES.` → `WEEK FIVE: THE BEGINNING.`

segments.voice: A crowded market. A parent turns around, and the child isn't there. The stomach drops. Every second becomes an hour. Now stretch that to three days. Every year, Luke says, Mary and Joseph walked to Jerusalem for the Passover, in a big crowd of relatives and neighbors. When Jesus is twelve, they start home, and assume he's somewhere in the caravan with the cousins. A whole day's walk later, they realize he isn't. They turn around. They search Jerusalem. One day. Two. Three. Today, Luke's story of Jesus at twelve.
screen: `YOU TURN AROUND. HE'S GONE.` → `A DAY'S WALK BEFORE THEY NOTICE.` → `ONE DAY. TWO. THREE.`

segments.voice: Here's where they find him, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "in the temple, sitting in the midst of the doctors, hearing them, and asking them questions." Doctors here means teachers, the scholars of the law. And a twelve-year-old boy from a village is sitting among them, listening and asking questions, and Luke says everyone was astonished at how he understood and how he answered. Mary says what a frightened parent says: "Son, why hast thou done so to us? behold thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing." Sorrowing. Three days of it. And his answer is the first thing Jesus ever says in Luke's Gospel: "How is it that you sought me? did you not know, that I must be about my father's business?" Here's a detail worth knowing. In Luke's Greek, the phrase is short and open: literally, in the things of my Father. Older English Bibles say my father's business. Some newer ones say my Father's house. Both are possible. Either way, he's saying: I'm where I belong. Luke adds, honestly, that they didn't understand what he meant. Even Mary. And then he goes home with them, and is obedient to them, and Mary keeps all these things in her heart, the same words Luke used after the shepherds. Catholics hold this story in two places at once. It's the fifth joyful mystery of the rosary: the finding in the Temple, a joy. And it's one of the seven sorrows of Mary: three days of searching. Notice where they found him. Not playing, not lost and crying. Asking questions. In this story, questions aren't the opposite of faith. The first time we meet Jesus as more than a baby, that's what he's doing.
screen: `SITTING AMONG THE TEACHERS.` · `THY FATHER AND I HAVE SOUGHT THEE.` · `IN THE THINGS OF MY FATHER.` · `A JOY AND A SORROW.` · then, large: `THEY FOUND HIM ASKING QUESTIONS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice for today's two-minute sit. Think of a time you lost someone. Maybe for a few minutes in a crowd. Maybe for years, to a falling-out. Maybe for good. Let yourself remember what the searching felt like. Don't hurry past it. Then, if they were found, remember that moment too. If they weren't, just hold them gently. If you pray, you can bring them to God. The bell holds the time.
Lost for three days. The boy Jesus in the Temple, found among the teachers, listening and asking questions.
Your line: they found him asking questions. Today, ask one real question about something you've always just accepted, and listen to the answer. Day twenty-nine.

30.title: The hidden years
30.hook: thirty years in Nazareth, a trade, a village, nothing written down
30.carry: most of his life was ordinary
30.howItsDone: Catholics honor the hidden life of Jesus on the feast of the Holy Family, after Christmas, and on the feast of Saint Joseph the Worker, May 1; many religious communities take Nazareth as a model of prayerful ordinary work.

segments.voice: Yesterday, lost for three days, and found in the Temple. Your line was: they found him asking questions. What did you ask? Today, what comes after that story: almost nothing at all. Day thirty.

A biography keeps the graduation, the wedding, the big move. It skips the ten thousand Tuesdays: the dishes, the commute, the afternoon someone fixed a chair. Now look at the Gospels. There's the birth. There's one story at twelve. And then the story jumps. The next time we see Jesus, Luke says he's about thirty years old. Between twelve and thirty, nothing. About eighteen years without a single scene. Catholics have a name for that silence. They call it the hidden life. Today, the hidden years.
screen: `NOT THE TEN THOUSAND TUESDAYS.` → `TWELVE, THEN THIRTY.` → `EIGHTEEN YEARS, NO SCENES.`

segments.voice: Let's be honest about what we know, because it's very little. Luke gives two sentences. In the Douay-Rheims Bible: "And he went down with them, and came to Nazareth, and was subject to them." And then: "Jesus advanced in wisdom, and age, and grace with God and men." Grace, your first word, again. He grew, the way children grow. That's it. Mark adds one clue, years later, when the people of Nazareth are offended by him: "Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary?" The Greek word is tekton, a builder, a craftsman who works with wood or stone. So we can guess at a life: a small village, a family trade, likely learned from Joseph. Rough hands. Customers who paid late. Weddings and funerals of neighbors. Probably Joseph's death somewhere in there, since he disappears from the story. But those are guesses. The Gospels are silent, and it's worth saying so. Later writers couldn't stand the silence. Later, stories appeared of a boy Jesus making clay birds fly and doing flashy miracles. The Church never accepted those as scripture. The real tradition kept the silence, and found something in it. Catholics say this: if Jesus is who they believe he is, then God spent about thirty years, of a life tradition counts at about thirty-three, doing ordinary work in a village no one had heard of. Most of his life was hidden, and it wasn't wasted. A French hermit named Charles de Foucauld, now a saint, spent years trying to live just like that, and called it living Nazareth. The ordinary counts. Sawing a board carefully counts.
screen: `TWO SENTENCES FROM LUKE.` · `IS NOT THIS THE CARPENTER?` · `THE GOSPELS ARE SILENT.` · `LIVING NAZARETH.` · then, large: `MOST OF HIS LIFE WAS ORDINARY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice for today's two-minute sit. Think about the most ordinary thing you'll do today. Washing a pan. Answering emails. Driving the same road. Folding a shirt. Picture yourself doing it slowly and well, with full attention, the way a craftsman planes a board. No one will see. That's the point. Let the whole sit rest on that one ordinary task. If you pray, you can offer it to God before you start. The bell holds the time.
The hidden years. About eighteen silent years in Nazareth: a trade, a village, and nothing written down.
Your line: most of his life was ordinary. Today, do your ordinary work carefully, one piece of it at least, as if it matters. Catholics would say it does. Day thirty.

31.title: The voice in the desert (Matthew 3:1–12)
31.hook: John the Baptist in camel hair, eating locusts, calling people to turn around
31.howItsDone: Catholics hear John the Baptist's call in the Advent Sunday readings and answer it in the sacrament of penance (confession), where a person names their sins, receives absolution and is given a penance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hidden years: thirty years in Nazareth, and almost nothing written down. Your line was most of his life was ordinary. What ordinary thing did you do carefully? Day thirty-one. Today the quiet ends, with a shout from the desert.

Out past the towns, in the dry country near the Jordan River, a man is shouting. He wears a rough garment of camel's hair with a leather belt. He eats locusts and wild honey. No house, no title, no invitation. And people come. Matthew says they came out from Jerusalem and all Judea and the whole region around the Jordan, out into the dry country to hear him. They stood in the river, confessed their sins, and he baptized them in the water. This is John, the one Christians call the Baptist. He's a relative of Jesus, and his message fits in one breath. Today: what he was shouting, and the road he wanted built.
screen: `A MAN SHOUTING IN THE DESERT.` → `CAMEL HAIR, LOCUSTS, WILD HONEY.` → `AND THE CROWDS COME.`

segments.voice: Here is John's message in the Douay-Rheims Bible, the old Catholic English translation: "Do penance: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand." The King James says repent. Both are reaching for one Greek word, metanoia. Meta, after or beyond. Noia, from the word for mind. A change of mind. A turning around. Not a feeling bad, first of all. A new direction. The Douay-Rheims followed the Latin Bible, which says do penance, and that wording is one reason Catholics speak of the sacrament of penance: confession carries an echo of this call to turn. Then Matthew reaches back to the prophet Isaiah, centuries earlier, and hears John in it: "A voice of one crying in the desert, Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make straight his paths." Isaiah's picture is a road made ready for a king: the low places filled, the hills brought down, the crooked made straight. John says: a king is coming, and the road is you. And John is not gentle about it. When religious leaders come to watch, he tells them to bring forth fruit worthy of penance, to show the turning in how they live. The axe, he says, is already at the root of the trees. But he points away from himself. Someone mightier is coming after him, he says, and he isn't worthy even to carry his sandals. The Church keeps John close. His voice fills the Sundays of Advent, and his birth has its own feast, on June twenty-fourth, as well as his death.
screen: `DO PENANCE: THE KINGDOM IS AT HAND.` · `METANOIA — A CHANGE OF MIND.` · `A KING IS COMING. FIX THE ROAD.` · `HE POINTS AWAY FROM HIMSELF.` · then, large: `PREPARE YE THE WAY OF THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one thing to turn from. Settle, and let your breathing slow. Not your whole life. One thing. A habit that keeps making the road crooked. A sharp way you talk to someone. A scroll you can't stop. A grudge you keep feeding. Find it and name it, plainly, inside. You don't have to fix it now. Just turn and face it. If you pray, you can hold it up to God and ask for help turning. If you don't, just sit with the naming. The bell holds the time.
The voice in the desert. John the Baptist, calling people to turn around and make the road ready for someone greater. Today's word.
screen: `THE VOICE IN THE DESERT — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: make straight the way. Today, straighten one small crooked thing: a message you owe, an apology, a promise you let slide. Fill one pothole. Day thirty-one.

32.title: The baptism (Matthew 3:13–17)
32.hook: Jesus steps into the line of sinners, the sky opens, a voice says beloved
32.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the Baptism of the Lord as the feast that ends the Christmas season, pray it as the first Luminous Mystery of the rosary, and bless themselves with holy water on entering a church as a reminder of their own baptism.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the voice in the desert: John at the river, calling people to turn around. Your line was make straight the way. Did you fill one pothole? Day thirty-two.

Picture the riverbank. A long line of people waiting to go down into the water. Every one of them is there for the same reason: they've done things they regret, and they want to turn around. A tax man. A soldier. A woman who hasn't spoken to her sister in years. Nobody in that line is showing off. And then a carpenter from Nazareth steps into the line. He waits his turn like everybody else. When he reaches the front, John looks at him and stops. He knows who this is. And he tries to refuse. Today: the day Jesus got in line.
screen: `A LINE OF PEOPLE WITH REGRETS.` → `A CARPENTER STEPS INTO LINE.` → `JOHN TRIES TO REFUSE.`

segments.voice: John's words, in the Douay-Rheims: "I ought to be baptized by thee, and comest thou to me?" It's backward, he's saying. You should be baptizing me. Jesus answers that it is fitting, for now, to fulfill all justice, and John lets him come down into the river. Why would Jesus get in the line at all? Christians have asked that for two thousand years. The Church's answer is that he wasn't there for his own sins. He was standing where sinners stand, on purpose, in the water with them. Then the story opens up. As he comes out of the water, Matthew says, the heavens were opened, and he saw the Spirit of God coming down like a dove and resting on him. And a voice from heaven: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." Notice when the voice comes. Before a single miracle. Before one sermon, one follower, one healing. He hasn't done anything yet, and he's already beloved. The Church reads this scene as a window onto the Trinity: the Son in the water, the Spirit like a dove, the Father's voice. The feast of the Baptism of the Lord closes the Christmas season, and it's the first of the Luminous Mysteries of the rosary. And Catholics hear their own baptism in it. The Catechism teaches that baptism makes a person an adopted child of God. That's why there's holy water at the church door: people dip their fingers and make the sign of the cross on the way in, remembering the water they came through.
screen: `JOHN: YOU SHOULD BAPTIZE ME.` · `HE STANDS WHERE SINNERS STAND.` · `BELOVED, BEFORE HE DOES ANYTHING.` · `HOLY WATER AT THE CHURCH DOOR.` · then, large: `THIS IS MY BELOVED SON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: touch water and remember you are loved. If you can, get a little water: a glass, a tap, a bowl. Put your fingers in it. Feel how cold or warm it is. If you're Catholic, you might make the sign of the cross, the way people do at the church door. If not, just let the water be water. Now sit, and let one sentence rest on you: loved, before doing anything. Not for your work today. Not for what you'll get right. Just loved. The bell holds the time.
The baptism. Jesus steps into the river with sinners, and a voice from heaven calls him beloved. Today's word.
Your line: you are the beloved. Today, each time you wash your hands, let the water remind you of it. Loved first, before the day's work. Day thirty-two.

33.title: Forty days hungry (Matthew 4:1–11)
33.hook: bread, a leap, the kingdoms of the world, three temptations and three refusals
33.howItsDone: Catholics keep Lent as forty days of prayer, fasting and almsgiving; the Gospel on the First Sunday of Lent is the temptation in the desert, and many give up a comfort for the season.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the baptism: the sky opened and a voice said beloved. Your line was you are the beloved. Did the water remind you? Day thirty-three. And straight from the river, Matthew says, he goes into the desert.

Afterwards he was hungry. That's all Matthew says about forty days without food. Not a missed lunch: the kind of hunger where the head goes light and every thought bends toward bread. Matthew says Jesus was led by the spirit into the desert, fasted forty days and forty nights, and afterwards he was hungry. And that's exactly when the tempter comes. Not on day one, when he's strong. At the end, when he's weakest. Three offers, one after another. Today: three temptations, and three refusals.
screen: `FORTY DAYS, FORTY NIGHTS.` → `AFTERWARD HE WAS HUNGRY.` → `THEN THE TEMPTER COMES.`

segments.voice: The first offer is bread. If you are the Son of God, the tempter says, tell these stones to become loaves. It's reasonable. He's starving. And the answer, in the Douay-Rheims: "Not in bread alone doth man live, but in every word that proceedeth from the mouth of God." Bread matters. But you're more than a stomach. The second offer is a leap. The devil takes him to the highest point of the Temple and says: throw yourself down, and quotes a psalm about angels catching you. Even scripture can be used as bait. Jesus answers: you shall not tempt the Lord your God. Don't force God to prove himself. The third offer is everything. From a very high mountain, all the kingdoms of the world and their glory. All of it, if you bow down once. And the answer: "Begone, Satan: for it is written, The Lord thy God shalt thou adore, and him only shalt thou serve." Look up his three answers and they all come from the book of Deuteronomy, from Moses speaking to Israel after forty years in the wilderness. Israel was tested in the desert for forty years; Jesus for forty days, answering with Israel's own words. The Church builds a season on this story. Lent is forty days, and on the first Sunday of Lent the Gospel is the temptation in the desert. Catholics fast and give things up then, not because comfort is bad, but to find out what they're really living on.
screen: `STONES INTO BREAD.` · `THROW YOURSELF DOWN.` · `ALL THE KINGDOMS, FOR ONE BOW.` · `THREE ANSWERS FROM DEUTERONOMY.` · then, large: `NOT IN BREAD ALONE DOTH MAN LIVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the offer that pulls hardest. Settle and breathe. Run through the three offers once more. Bread: comfort, the easy fix. The leap: proof, being sure. The kingdoms: control, getting your way. Notice which one tugs hardest today, if any does. Don't judge it. Just name it, the way you'd name the weather. Then ask, gently: what else am I hungry for? If you pray, you can bring that hunger to God. The bell holds the time.
Forty days hungry. Jesus in the desert, tempted three times, answering each time with scripture. Today's word.
Your line: not by bread alone. When that offer shows up today, let the hunger ask its question: what am I really living on? Day thirty-three.

34.title: Launch out into the deep (Luke 5:1–11)
34.hook: Peter has fished all night for nothing and lets down the nets once more
34.howItsDone: Catholics hear this Gospel at Sunday Mass in the Lectionary's year of Luke, and "duc in altum" is a much-quoted motto since John Paul II used it in his 2001 letter for the new millennium.

segments.voice: Yesterday, forty days hungry in the desert, and three refusals. Your line was not by bread alone. What were you really hungry for? Day thirty-four.

Morning on the lake of Genesareth, the Sea of Galilee. Two boats pulled up on the shore. The fishermen are out of them, washing their nets, which is what you do after a long night. And it has been a long night. Simon and his partners have worked from dark to dawn and caught nothing. Not a small catch. Nothing. It's the shift that went nowhere, the job application with no reply, the effort with nothing to show. They're tired, and they want to go home. Then a crowd arrives, pressing around a teacher, and the teacher steps into Simon's boat. Today: what happens when you're asked to try once more.
screen: `ALL NIGHT, NOTHING.` → `WASHING THE EMPTY NETS.` → `A TEACHER STEPS INTO THE BOAT.`

segments.voice: Jesus asks Simon to push out a little from the land, and he teaches the crowd sitting in the boat. Then, when he's finished, he turns to Simon and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Launch out into the deep, and let down your nets for a draught." Simon is the expert here. He knows the lake. He's just spent the whole night at it. His answer is honest, and a little tired: "Master, we have laboured all the night, and have taken nothing: but at thy word I will let down the net." That word but is the hinge. Not because I think it'll work. Because you said so. And the nets fill so full they start to break. They wave to their partners in the other boat, James and John, and both boats fill until they begin to sink. Now look at Simon. He doesn't celebrate. He falls down at Jesus's knees and says: depart from me, for I am a sinful man. The catch has frightened him, not with danger, but with nearness. And Jesus answers: fear not, from now on you'll be catching people. They bring the boats to land, leave everything, and follow him. In the Latin Bible, the line opens with three short words: duc in altum. Pope John Paul the Second used it to open the new millennium, calling the whole Church to launch out into the deep. Simon, of course, is the one the Church will call Peter.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one thing you've stopped trying at. Settle and breathe. Let it come to mind: a conversation that never goes well, a habit you keep failing to start, a hope you put down. Don't pick the biggest. Pick one you could try once more today. Hear Simon's sentence, and let it be yours if it fits: I've worked all night and caught nothing, but I'll let down the net. If you pray, you can offer the trying to God. The bell holds the time.
Launch out into the deep. A tired fisherman lets down his nets once more, at someone else's word. Today's word.

35.title: The wine ran out (John 2:1–11)
35.hook: at a wedding in Cana Mary tells the servants whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye
35.howItsDone: Catholics pray the wedding at Cana as the second Luminous Mystery of the rosary and often read it at weddings; Mary's words to the servants are a favorite line for describing her role of pointing to her son.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a tired fisherman heard launch out into the deep, and the nets nearly broke. Did you try the one thing once more? Day thirty-five, the last day of the week. It ends at a party.

A village wedding in Galilee. Not an afternoon reception: a feast, guests eating and drinking, and the family's honor riding on every cup. Jesus is there, with his first few followers. His mother is there too. And then, somewhere in the middle of it, the thing a host dreads. The wine runs out. The guests don't know yet. The bridegroom may not know yet. But someone has noticed. Not the host, not the steward. Mary. Today: the first sign in John's Gospel, and the woman who saw the need first.

segments.voice: Mary goes to her son with four words, in the Douay-Rheims: "They have no wine." She doesn't tell him what to do. She just names the need. His answer sounds cool to our ears: "Woman, what is that to me and to thee? my hour is not yet come." Woman wasn't rude in his language. It's the same word he'll use for her from the cross. But he's saying: this isn't my moment. And Mary doesn't argue. She turns to the servants and says: "Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye." Then she steps out of the story. There are six stone water jars standing there, for the Jewish washing rites, holding two or three measures apiece, John says. A great deal of water. Jesus tells the servants: fill them with water. They fill them to the brim. Draw some out, he says, and take it to the chief steward. The steward tastes it, doesn't know where it came from, and calls the bridegroom over, puzzled: everyone serves the good wine first, and the cheap stuff once people have had plenty. "But thou hast kept the good wine until now." Six jars of it. John calls this the beginning of his signs. Catholics treasure it for Mary's sake. Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye: they're the last words John's Gospel gives her, and they point away from herself. Here Catholics see why they ask Mary to pray for them. She notices the need, brings it to her son, and tells everyone else to listen to him. It's the second Luminous Mystery of the rosary.

segments.voice: Here's the practice, and a look back. This week began with a boy lost for three days, then the hidden years, the voice in the desert, the baptism, forty days hungry, and the nets at dawn. Now the wine. Settle and breathe. Think of the rooms you'll be in today: home, work, a group chat. Is there a need nobody has named? Someone running out of something: patience, money, company, hope. Just notice it. If you pray, you can do what Mary did and simply say it: they have no wine. The bell holds the time.
The wine ran out. A wedding at Cana, a mother who noticed, and the first of his signs. Today's word.
Your line: do whatever he tells you. Today, when you notice a need, bring it to someone who can help, and then help the way you're asked to. Day thirty-five. Next week: healings and encounters.
